extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper reporters writing feature stories and event coverage (parades, ceremonies, charity drives, performances)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplar pieces for reporting public ceremonies, parades, charity events, theatrical pantomimes and human-interest holiday stories; emphasizes scene-setting, human detail, organization names/numbers, and performance description. Useful for reporters preparing feature copy for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight the most remarkable sight as a lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with the striking observation or most remarkable sight of the occasion to grab reader attention (e.g., 'Many persons thought this the most remarkable sight of the evening' — the neat, roomy Fifth avenue roadway with no traffic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a single vivid image or observation from the scene as an entry point. The example contrasts the usual busy avenue with an unusual empty roadway — an effective lead. Avoid generic leads; choose the moment readers will remember.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include concrete statistics and counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Report numeric facts about the event (attendance figures, counts of participants, prize amounts) such as 'More than 2,000 automobiles and trucks and 1,000 motorcycles were in line' and 'Prizes worth more than $6,000 had been offered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise numbers where available to give scale and credibility. Use qualifiers (more than, about) when exact counts are uncertain. Include prize values, lists of units, and crowd estimates to quantify the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid anecdotal and colorful detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Include humanizing, often comic or striking anecdotes and visual details (women in decorative cars failing to put on the same amount of clothes they'd wear to the opera; a man coming up smiling from a big bathtub who on closer view was 'wearing tights').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes and quirky visuals bring features to life. Select tidbits that reveal character, contrast, or irony and that illustrate the event without derailing factual reporting. Keep tone appropriate to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey atmosphere and weather as scene-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe weather and atmospheric conditions and how they affect participants and spectators (examples: 'the sky cloudless and the sun shining brilliantly,' 'breezes from the Hudson River kept the marchers and the spectators cool').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weather can influence mood, attendance, and comfort — include it early if it shaped the event. Use sensory verbs (whistled, moaned, kept cool) to situate readers on the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify participants, officials and their titles
rubrics_metrics.description: List and identify key persons and officeholders present, with ranks/titles when relevant (e.g., Grand Marshal, Rear Admirals, Major Gen. John F. O'Ryan, Governor Glynn, Mayor Mitchel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming prominent figures and their roles grounds the story in authority and ceremony. When listing many names, group by role or function to preserve readability; include only those whose presence matters to the reader or the event's significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report order and organization of processions/pageantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the sequence and composition of marching units and divisions (mounted police at the head, battalions, First Division of the National Guard, Grand Army posts, bands, fife and drum corps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect to know who led, who followed, and notable units. Convey the procession's structure and any noteworthy formations or honors. Use this to show scale and ceremonial order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations from participants for human voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Include participants' own words to humanize the piece (example: George Sebech: 'I am 98 years old, but I'll be marching here ten years from now...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, telling quotes reveal personality and emotion; attribute them clearly. Choose quotes that illuminate motive, feeling, or character rather than restating facts the reporter can provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight symbolism and crowd reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize symbolic elements (flags, uniforms, medals) and record the audience's emotional response (cheers, applause, ovations) such as 'The flag display ... was the greatest the city has seen' and 'Receiving cheers and shouts of encouragement at every block.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols convey meaning beyond facts; describe them and their effect on the crowd. Record audible reactions and visual displays to communicate communal sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report organizational details and charity logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering charitable or civic services, list the organizations involved, quantities distributed, beneficiaries and logistics (e.g., Salvation Army, Central Union Mission, Almas Temple giving away 500 baskets, Associated Charities arranging baskets, vans provided by a bank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers need to know who ran the effort, how aid was delivered, and who benefited. Include numbers of baskets/meals, coordinating groups, locations, and any volunteer involvement (e.g., Boy Scouts distributing gifts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize performance content and characters
rubrics_metrics.description: For theatrical or pantomime coverage, provide a concise synopsis of the plot and list principal characters and who played them (example: 'The Seven Gifts, a Fantasy of Christmas Giving' with Wanderer, Emerald Queen, Jack-in-the-Box, Pierrot, Moon Lady, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give enough plot and character detail so readers unfamiliar with the work understand the action and its highlights. Note standout moments or the thematic core (e.g., the child's heartfelt gift being the most valuable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include technical and staging details
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention lighting, stagecraft and logistics that affected the performance ('arc lights in the park had been turned off... concealed lights on the stage lit up the blue scenery,' placards announcing action so 'all might understand').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage and technical details help readers visualize the production and explain limitations or creative choices. Note what enhanced or hindered audience experience (crowding, lighting, space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke emotional imagery and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use evocative metaphors and images to convey emotion and appearance (children with 'little red wrappers over their nighties... looked for all the world like little animated red holly berries').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-chosen metaphor paints a memorable picture and compresses complex feeling. Use such language sparingly and appropriately for the tone of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute roles to organizers, staff and contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit the people and groups who organized or contributed to the event (nurses and teachers at hospitals, Miss Mary V. Merrick directing Christ Child Society work, Miss Laura B. Anderson the nurse in charge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing organizers and contributors shows accountability and gives readers names to connect with the work. Include positions and specific contributions when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame human-interest stories with resilience and uplift
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight stories of courage, recovery or community care (crippled children performing cheerfully, elderly veterans marching despite age and wounds, sick children joyfully receiving gifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature copy often emphasizes inspiration; balance uplift with respect for subjects' dignity. Use concrete examples of resilience rather than platitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue and dialect selectively to capture authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short, colloquial exchanges that reveal character and immediacy (children's dialectal speech: 'I gotta chu-chu... I gotta dawg.'; hospital child's 'Sure... there's goin' to be a show').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue adds realism and voice but should be used sparingly and transcribed accurately. Preserve pronunciation only when it contributes meaning or characterization and avoid caricature.
